The variational search found the exact lowest energy of H2, -1.137306 hartree. The number that came back from IQM's test device was -0.163 hartree. That number does not describe the molecule. The test device returns made-up counts that ignore the circuit you send.

What I ran: I wrote H2 at 0.735 angstrom in the STO-3G model as a 2-qubit energy formula. The formula has 5 parts with fixed weights: a constant, Z on qubit 0, Z on qubit 1, Z on both qubits, and X on both qubits. I added the 0.7200 hartree repulsion between the two nuclei. The circuit has one adjustable angle theta. It flips qubit 0, rotates qubit 1 by theta, and links the two with a CNOT gate. This mixes the simple starting guess (the Hartree-Fock state) with one other arrangement of the electrons.

The variational step: I first tried 61 values of theta on an error-free simulator on this computer. Then I refined the best one and kept theta = -0.2235. At theta = 0 the circuit gives the Hartree-Fock energy of -1.116999 hartree. At the best theta the simulated energy is -1.137306 hartree. That equals the exact answer from solving the 4x4 energy matrix directly, to within about 1e-15 hartree. The search lowered the energy by about 0.020 hartree. That gain is the effect of the electrons avoiding each other, which the simple starting guess leaves out.

The final job: Job 01a1603f-6b7b-7179-b94c-c353e7ede231 ran on garnet:mock with 4000 shots and finished with status DONE. It held two circuits. The first measured the qubits directly, for the Z parts. The second added a Hadamard gate on each qubit first, for the X part. A perfect device would return mostly 01 and 10 in the first circuit. The mock returned 00 and 11 about half each in both circuits (Z circuit: 00=1979, 11=2021. X circuit: 00=2004, 11=1996). Those counts give -0.163 hartree. The gap from the exact value comes from the mock's fake counts. It says nothing about the method. On a real device such as Garnet, noise would also move the result away from -1.137, and error mitigation would be needed to get close.

The principle is the variational principle. No setting of the circuit can give an energy below the true lowest energy. So you can try settings, keep the one with the lowest energy, and know you are moving toward the answer. A quantum computer prepares the state and measures the energy. A normal computer picks the next setting to try.

Caveat: I used the standard published Hamiltonian weights for H2 at 0.735 angstrom (parity mapping with two-qubit reduction). I did not compute them from scratch, because no chemistry package is installed here. The exact energy they give, -1.137306 hartree, matches the known textbook value.
